content_html:
Earlier this year I wrote a post on yk, which can automatically add JIT compilers to C interpreters. Since then we’ve applied yk to more interpreters, fixed various bugs, and improved performance notably. Towards the end of October I showed some data where on our benchmark suite1 yklua is 2× faster than the PUC Lua interpreter it takes as a base.

I was quite pleased with myself until someone brought me down to earth by asking “how do you know if this works for large interpreters?” It’s a fair question: PUC Lua is at least an order of magnitude smaller2 than CPython or CRuby and who’s to say if it would work with much bigger interpreters? We had looked at CPython a year or so ago, but at that point yk was missing several obvious things that CPython would need, so we quickly moved on. A lot has changed since then, and a quick LLM experiment got far enough to suggest it would be worth looking again.

Happily, having taken a deeper look, CPython not only works when adapted for yk as ykcpython3, but there are meaningful performance gains to be had — not only relative to normal CPython, but also relative to Python’s experimental JIT4. Roughly speaking, this is the result of 3-4 days’ work on ykcpython directly; there was a separate week and a half of generic yk bug fixing necessary to get to the point that I could look at ykcpython itself.

Here are the “final” numbers from my brief odyssey on ykcpython and the AWFY benchmark suite:

A simple summary of the table is: ykcpython is faster than cpython on every benchmark except DeltaBlue (where it’s about 2.5% slower); and faster than cpython_jit on 8 out of 13 benchmarks.

The point of this post is not to pretend that ykcpython is in any way ready for people to use — it definitely is not! Nor is it to pretend that one can expect performance on a wider set of programs to be as good as the numbers above — it definitely won’t! My view is that benchmark suite performance is a hoop to jump through rather than an end in itself: a system which benchmarks well might perform poorly in the real world; but a system which benchmarks poorly nearly always performs poorly in the real world.

Rather, I wanted to use this post as a way of showing what it’s like to adapt an interpreter for yk5: the stages I went through; and to give a sense of how the just under 450LoC I added were enough to achieve a meaningful effect. Luckily I had a sense that this might be a useful journey, so I was able to write enough stuff down to be able to flesh out this full post.

A quick refresher

If you haven’t read the earlier yk post, here’s a very brief refresher. Given a lightly modified C interpreter6 as input, yk produces a VM with a meta-tracing JIT compiler as output7. yk doesn’t aim to produce the fastest possible JIT compiling language implementation: rather, it aims to make the language implementation you know and love somewhat faster while retaining 100% compatibility. Put another way a “ykified” interpreter is a fork of the existing C version of the interpreter, with (hopefully!) a handful of adjustments.

As with any meta-tracing JIT compiler, yk identifies hot loops in the guest language (e.g. Lua or Python), and traces the interpreter (i.e. records what the C code is executing while it is interpreting the guest language). It then optimises those traces and converts them to machine code.

yk requires interpreters to tell it where potential loops in the guest language are via the YkLocation struct. Optionally – though if you want to get good performance, definitely necessary! – interpreter authors can add optimisation hints that embed knowledge about the language or its common idioms of use such as “at this point this seemingly dynamic value almost never changes”. In general, working out where to put YkLocations is relatively easy, but working out where to put hints requires a much greater understanding of the interpreter, and careful measurement to understand which do and don’t help.

The challenge I face when adapting an interpreter for yk is that I rarely know the interpreter well, if at all. Rather than trying to do everything at once, I have learnt to start off as simple as possible: I try and do the minimum changes that lead to some traces being recorded and compiled to machine code. This can be trickier than it seems: I’ve got to understand the build system8, and work out where to put some semi-sensible YkLocations. I’ve also learnt to make sure that the language’s test suite works from this very first step: keeping it working thereafter is not only much easier, but it lessens the number of times one attempts optimisations that are unsound.

For a simple interpreter, you might get a basic JIT compiler from an interpreter with fewer than 10LoC (Lines-of-Code) changed. For somewhat bigger interpreters, a few more changes tend to be necessary. For example, yk doesn’t like “threaded” interpreters that use goto between opcodes, because it doesn’t give it enough opportunities to intercede and see what’s going on. Fortunately, such changes are not generally too big.

Finding the right starting point

Since it had been a long time since I looked at CPython’s internals9, I started with the part I was vaguely familiar with. As I later discovered, this is now called the “tier 1” interpreter. Quickly hacking in support for yk highlighted several missing things in yk (from basic atomic loads to not-implemented-bit-widths in sub, minor incompatibilities (e.g. reading an environment variable after a CPython test had wiped it), and flat out bugs (from stackmap fixes to not doing silly things after fork). Fixing all those took me around a week and a half; I’m not going to talk about them in detail in this post, because they’re generic fixes that aren’t ykcpython specific.

My adaption of the tier 1 interpreter is deliberately minimalistic. Most of the changes in the 200LoC diff are small one-offs that aren’t hugely interesting: we need CPython to use its (builtin but non-default) switch-based interpreter; and yk uses a shadow stack, so CPython’s C stack resizing needs to take that into account too. The most interesting thing I did was to add YkLocations at backwards jump opcodes, which I expected to be enough for some half-sensible traces to be created.

I wasn’t expecting this first version of ykcpython to be faster than CPython – if nothing else, it contained almost no optimisation hints – but it was much slower than I expected. It was definitely creating traces, and they were executing correctly – the test suite passed, albeit taking more memory than I’d like10 – but something clearly wasn’t right.

Fortunately, it didn’t take very long to work out what. 4 years ago, CPython added support for quickening under the heading of “specialisation”. Quickening is a simple, clever technique for improving interpreter performance that rewrites “generic” opcodes (e.g. “add objects”) to “specialised”, faster, opcodes (e.g. “add two ints”) when possible, deoptimising back to the generic opcodes if necessary. I tend to think of quickening as giving a decent portion of the benefit of a JIT compiler without all the bother of generating machine code11. The problem for yk is that sometimes a program’s opcodes can transition between specialised and unspecialised opcodes a large number of times, and the simple way I’d added yk support meant that each transition implicitly threw away the associated trace and created a new one. In most cases, traces weren’t used long enough to overcome the cost of creating them.

There are techniques which can overcome this problem, and I did briefly experiment with them, but I then recalled a conversation I had with some CPython developers last year. A quick look inside CPython confirmed my recollection: CPython contains a “tier 2” interpreter as well. This isn’t a completely new interpreter; rather it is an alternative implementation of core parts of the main interpreter loop, mostly intended for CPython’s experimental JIT compiler.

A very quick experiment later suggested that the tier 2 interpreter was – at least at a basic level – a better fit for yk12. I thus ripped out the tier 1 support and added support for yk in the tier 2 interpreter. Happily, tier 2 support is even easier than tier 1 support, consisting of a mere 80 LoC. To give you a quick idea of what yk support looks like, here’s the part that attaches YkLocations13 to the (start of) loops:

for (uint32_t i = 0; i < executor->code_size; i++) {
  const _PyUOpInstruction *uop = &executor->trace[i];
  if (_PyUop_Uncached[uop->opcode] == _JUMP_TO_TOP) {
    uint16_t target = uop_get_jump_target(uop);
    if (yk_location_is_null(executor->yk_locs[target])) {
      executor->yk_locs[target] = yk_location_new();
    }
  }
}

For the rest of this post, I’m going to be using yk and the tier 2 interpreter as the starting point for ykcpython.

What’s being benchmarked

When optimising any language implementation, it’s important to know where its performance sits in the wider performance landscape. To understand how ykcpython was doing, I used two other baselines: “stock” CPython; and CPython with the experimental JIT. I configured cpython as follows:

CC=clang-21 CXX=clang++-21 \
  ./configure \
  --enable-optimizations \
  --with-lto

Note that I’m deliberately using the same version of LLVM for both cpython and cpython_jit because the latter requires LLVM-21. ykllvm – the fork of LLVM used in yk – is based off a version of LLVM about 6 months later than LLVM-21. That might slightly distort comparisons, but it’s a small enough difference that the effects hopefully are fairly minor. Bearing that in mind, ykcpython is configured as follows:

../configure \
  --without-computed-gotos \
  --without-tail-call-interp \
  --enable-experimental-jit=interpreter \
  --without-ensurepip

I used our fork14 of the AWFY benchmark suite, simply because I know how to run it without thinking.

The next challenge is to define a metric, or metrics, to report performance. Every metric has the potential to mislead and many are difficult to understand. In my opinion, the least worst single metric is wall-clock time: how long does my program take to run from start to finish? This doesn’t capture everything we want to know, but it captures a lot, and it’s easy to understand.

Most importantly this metric implicitly includes start-up and warm-up time. In other words I’m deliberately choosing a timing metric which tends to favour normal interpreters and “penalise” JIT compilers. To somewhat offset that, we run each AWFY benchmark for 10 in-process iterations (i.e. run the whole benchmark in a for 0..10 loop) so that we also get some sense of how optimisation benefits longer-running programs.

The big performance table at the start of this post uses a custom benchmark runner on an idle machine. All the timings from now on in the post are from me running time once as a normal user without being too careful if the machine is completely idle or not: when starting to optimise an interpreter, it’s not practical to wait an hour to benchmark every change on many benchmarks, when the effects are generally quite large15.

Optimising interpreter dispatch

There are various ways one can go about optimising an interpreter for meta-tracing, all of which have pros and cons: the sequence of optimisations I’m showing here is just one way of going about things16.

There are a couple of useful things to notice here. First, we can see warm-up occurring: ykcpython’s first iteration is slower than subsequent iterations. That’s OK in my book: yk isn’t really intended for programs running in a fraction of a second. Second, the 102% cpu and user time that is higher than wall-clock time are due to yk running trace compilation in threads. That allows the interpreter to continue executing, reducing perceived pauses.

The first thing I do in this situation is look at the “high-level IR” (HIR) of the traces that yk has produced to see if things look sensible:

$ YKD_LOG_IR=/tmp/l1:hir ykcpython harness.py Mandelbrot 10 500
...
$ rg Begin /tmp/l1 | wc -l
11
$ rg Loop /tmp/l1 | wc -l

The logfile contains 11 traces, of which 1 is a “loop” trace. In general, loop traces are where yk is most effective, and the non-loop traces are the price we have to pay to get the promised land of loop traces. In this case, a simple profile showed that most execution time is spent in the solitary loop trace, which is a promising start for yk.

My first port of call when optimising an interpreter is to tackle interpreter dispatch. When an interpreter is executing a program, it continually asks “what is the opcode of the current instruction? Is it an add or a sub or …?” and then it dispatches to the code that performs the appropriate action. It’s probable that a large chunk of that 20KLoC of HIR is the interpreter loading an opcode from memory and checking what kind it is. yk’s trace optimiser has various classic compiler tricks up its sleeve, but in this case they don’t really help, because in most cases between the same instruction being loaded twice from memory, some other code will be called that yk has to assume might have mutated that memory. This isn’t unnecessary conservatism: Python programs really can mutate their function’s instructions!

I was particularly lucky because the tier2 interpreter uses “executors” which are traces of (optimised) instructions. Those instructions are immutable in the context of a given executor: should a Python function’s instructions change, any associated executors will be invalidated. That means that we can attach a simple monotonically increasing integer code ID to a _PyExecutorObject and know that for a given code ID, an opcode at index I will always be the same.

This allows us to use the single most effective optimisation hint in yk: idempotent functions. In essence, an idempotent function says “for the same inputs this function will always produce the same output”18. “Always” here really means “always”! Idempotent is a very strong guarantee that yk cannot help you uphold: if you fail to do so, your system will go wrong in weird ways.

Although yk provides a helper yk_idempotent_load function, we need something more specialised. Fortunately it’s not hard to write what we need:

__attribute__((yk_idempotent))
uint16_t idempotent_load_opcode(uint64_t code_id, const _PyUOpInstruction *pc)
{
    __asm__ volatile("" : "+r"(code_id));
    return pc->opcode;
}

Unsurprisingly, the yk_idempotent attribute tells yk that idempotent_load_opcode is an idempotent function. That means that if, in a particular trace, the function is called with parameters that are constant values then yk can remove the idempotent function call and replace it with its output. The __asm__ line is there to encourage LLVM not to inline the function19 (if the function is inlined, yk no longer knows there is anything idempotent there).

Using this requires changing just a few lines in the core interpreter loop. The most important lines are simply this:

yk_promote(next_uop);
yk_promote_code_id(yk_code_id);
uopcode = idempotent_load_opcode(yk_code_id, next_uop);

Promotion (e.g. yk_promote)20 says “this variable is expected to be semi-constant: record its concrete value and specialise the trace to it, but insert a guard in case that value later changes”. Imagine I have yk_promote(x) and when a trace is later recorded, x happens to be 3. The trace will record guard true (x == 3): if on later runs x is not 3, the guard will fail and the trace will deoptimise; if the guard succeeds we know henceforth that x is definitely 3.

In other words, in the context of the traces we’re recording, yk will see calls to idempotent_load_opcode with constant arguments, allowing it to replace the function call with a constant result. The point of this isn’t just to remove the cost of a load: rather, exposing constant data to yk’s trace optimiser allows it to do a much better job of optimising traces. In other words, a simple PR that changes 30LoC has made this benchmark over twice as fast as CPython and 25% faster than CPython’s JIT. Another way of judging the effectiveness of this optimisation is that it has reduced the 20,772 lines of HIR output to 7,648 lines21.

Code needs to be traced to be optimised

However, before we get carried away, this isn’t enough to make all benchmarks magically quicker. I have learnt from experience to rotate between benchmarks to avoid over-training22. In this case I decided to look at the deltablue benchmark, which I know from yklua can be a tough target. The situation in ykcpython turned out to be worse than I expected: cpython takes 7.67s, cpython_jit takes 6.20s, and ykcpython (with our idempotent change) takes 37.51s. Ouch!

My next port of call is to run YKD_LOG=2 which prints warnings if a trace can’t be compiled. Sure enough:

$ ykcpython harness.py DeltaBlue 10 12000
Starting DeltaBlue benchmark ...
yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long
yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long
yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long
yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long
yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long
yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long
DeltaBlue: iterations=1 runtime: 3362822us
yk-warning: trace-compilation-aborted: Unimplemented: '%188 = atomicrmw or ptr %187, i64 16 seq_cst, align 8'
...

For now I’m going to skip “trace too long”. In essence yk has a fixed limit for “this trace looks to be so long that it’s probably not useful”. The limit was too low, so I increased it unilaterally before doing the work for this post. Exactly what the right value is I don’t know. Indeed, I think that this crude heuristic probably needs replacing with something more sophisticated: doing that is a problem for another day.

Let’s move onto the “unimplemented” warning: I haven’t got around to implementing complex atomic instructions yet, so as soon as one of those is encountered, yk has no choice but to give up on that trace entirely. If it happens to be a hot part of a benchmark, that can absolutely kill performance. In this case, happily, the atomicrmw warnings just so happened to come from functions which we really don’t want to inline into the trace anyway.

One of tracing’s virtues is that it aggressively inlines functions, but that can inline checks which fail too often on subsequent executions. For example, one function we inline by default is _PyObject_GC_Link which checks to see if enough objects have been allocated for garbage collection to be worth scheduling. If we’re unlucky, we may trace an iteration of a loop which happens to schedule garbage collection: in nearly every subsequent execution, the resulting guard will fail, and we’ll take a somewhat slower path. The solution here is to mark such functions as yk_outline:

__attribute__((yk_outline))
void _PyObject_GC_Link(PyObject *op) { ... }

Functions marked yk_outline become calls in a trace. There are probably a number of functions which should be marked as yk_outline, but I marked the two that happened to cause the aborted warnings and that also obviously we don’t want to include in a trace anyway. Doing so improved execution time to 36.63s (about 2.5% faster), so they’re clearly not the major cause of the slowdown in this case.

Just when I was starting to fret, profiling execution showed that, to my surprise, deltablue was only spending about half its running time in JIT-compiled code, where one would expect it to be spending 90%+. It turns out that the main reason for this is that not all executors have a _JUMP_TO_TOP opcode and weren’t being traced.

My quick fix was to add a YkLocation at the first opcode in an executor. The one line fix does just that: it means that yk starts tracing as soon as it enters an executor. Doing so improves deltablue’s execution time to 8.64s (4.23× faster than before). That’s still 1.13× CPython, but it’s a lot better than before!

At the time I made this change I didn’t fully think about how adding a YkLocation at the start of an executor might interact with the YkLocation already added to _JUMP_TO_TOP. As luck would have it, I accidentally stumbled on a reasonable combination: _JUMP_TO_TOP tends to jump to the instruction at index 1. Still, I suspect that there might be a better way to add YkLocations to executors, but one can’t solve every problem all at once: it’s time to move onto the next thing!

Further into interpreter dispatch

Our earlier use of idempotent loads made such a huge impact on interpreter dispatch that it’s easy to overlook that it was a simple, shallow, change: it only optimised loading an instruction’s opcode kind. Instructions contain a number of other fields that are equally amenable to idempotent loading.

There are various ways one can go about optimising these additional fields. I could, for example, have replaced the definitions of some static functions in header files. To keep things simple, I defined a macro which can generate the two-parameter functions we need, and then nobbled some other macros to call it at appropriate points. With the resulting change deltablue’s performance improves to 8.09s — we’re now within 10% of cpython’s performance.

Unrolling

As we saw earlier, not all functions are good candidates for inlining into a trace. yk has a very simple heuristic – stolen shamelessly from RPython/PyPy – which is to mark functions containing loops as “outlined”. In other words, if C calls a function f() and f contains for (...) { ... } then yk will not inline calls to f.

The fundamental reason not to inline functions-with-loops is that tracing unrolls loops, and that tends not to be a good idea. First, some loops execute vast numbers of iterations, which would cause counter-productively-long traces. Second, loops’ iterations are often controlled by dynamic, ever-changing values: unrolling would specialise the trace to just one of those values, giving suboptimal performance on every other value.

There are however a small number of functions in an interpreter which we actively want to unroll. Typically those functions’ loops satisfy two properties: they only run a small number of iterations; and the number of iterations depends on an aspect of the user’s program that changes rarely. For example, a function called unpack_args(int num_args) which contains for (int i=0; i<num_args; i++) would be an excellent candidate, since it probably unpacks the same number of parameters every time it is called at the same place in a trace.

yk thus provides a yk_unroll attribute, which informs yk that a function that might otherwise be outlined should in fact be inlined and its loops unrolled. Rather than slog through every function in CPython looking for candidates, I did a simple grep/sort in hir to see which (implicitly non-inlined) C functions appear most often in traces23:

$ YKD_LOG_IR=/tmp/l1:hir ykcpython harness.py Json 10 100
...
$ rg call /tmp/l1|grep "@"|cut -d "@" -f 2|sort|uniq -c|sort -n
   2 PyLong_FromLong
   6 _Py_HandlePending
   6 do_lookup
  24 _PyList_FromStackRefStealOnSuccess
  50 _PyEvalFramePushAndInit
  50 _PyObject_GC_Link
  50 _PyObject_InitInlineValues

1035 _PyFrame_Initialize.5328
1158 _PyFrame_ClearLocals
1194 bcmp

bcmp is the standard libc function: all of the other functions are in CPython itself. Not all of those functions will have loops in them, but the chances are that most do. What I do in such a situation is go down (or, depending how you look at it, up) the list and look at the code in each function. I did that for a couple of benchmarks to ensure I got some coverage of common functions.

The two most commonly called CPython functions immediately looked like good candidates. _PyFrame_Initialize is the most obvious of the two, containing almost exactly the pattern I most like to match on:

_PyFrame_Initialize(..., int null_locals_from, ...) {
  ...
  for (int i = null_locals_from; i < code->co_nlocalsplus; i++) {
    frame->localsplus[i] = PyStackRef_NULL;
  }
  ...
}

_PyFrame_ClearLocals is slightly trickier: it contains a while loop involving pointer arithmetic, but it didn’t take me long to convince myself that it was a good candidate.

Earlier we made _PyObject_GC_Link not inlineable, so we don’t want to reverse that! Similarly, do_lookup looks values up in a dictionary, so we want to keep that outlined: it depends on an often-changing dynamic value.

PyLong_FromSsize_t and PyLong_FromLong were harder to judge. These functions’ inner loops depend on dynamic values, but my best guess is that they tend to be fairly stable in practice. I will be keeping an eye on these functions in the future, because I only have medium confidence that I made the right initial call.

As these examples suggest, I am generally fairly cautious about adding yk_unroll: inappropriate placings can easily help one benchmark and make many others worse. I thus tend to only mark one or two functions as yk_unroll, benchmark, and then move on. In this case, I did 5 small PRs, with the end effect that json went from 11.52s to 10.85s.

Indirect inlining

In general most function calls in C are direct: f() calls a function called f. However a minority of functions are indirect: f is a generic pointer whose value can be any compatible function. This is commonly used in interpreters to allow run-time dispatch to type specific code.

By default, yk cannot inline through indirect function calls, because without knowing exactly what pointer is being called, it can’t reliably reconstruct the path that execution took24. Fortunately, we already have the tool we need to solve this problem: yk_promote! If yk sees an indirect function call with a constant pointer it knows exactly what function is being called and can inline as normal. The common pattern I use is:

function_type f = ...;
if (!yk_is_interpreting())
  yk_promote(f);
(f)(...);

yk_is_interpreting() is true during “normal” interpretation; false during tracing; and (because it’s a constant false) removed during tracing. In other words, yk_promote is only called during the tracing phase. yk_is_interpreting() is fairly fast (much faster than yk_promote()) so this idiom is a small but useful performance win.

However, there is often a second problem. yk only puts the tracing machinery into a function if it can statically prove that it is reachable from a traceable path. Commonly, functions called from indirect calls cannot be statically proven to be traceable and thus they still leave an outlined call in the trace. We can solve that with the yk_indirect_inline function which tells yk “this function can be reached from an indirect call and should be considered for tracing”25.

Profiling a couple of benchmarks quickly showed several potential candidates26. My experience is that not all indirect call sites are good targets for promotion: for example, of the interpreters I’ve looked at so far, inlining malloc and free indirect calls has rarely been profitable. However, I quickly alighted upon a couple of promising candidates.

Let’s start with the less promising, but easier to explain, one: benchmarks like deltablue and json call len on lists and strings. Simplifying slightly, sq_length is a pointer to a function inside a CPython type, so this becomes an indirect call in traces. In the case of len([...]) the function that’s ultimately called is list_length:

static Py_ssize_t list_length(PyObject *a) {
  return PyList_GET_SIZE(a);
}

where PyList_GET_SIZE boils down (slightly elided) to a simple load a->ob_size. That’s the sort of code that yk loves to see inlined in a trace!

The resulting PR has to do a slightly annoying dance to make yk accept the yk_promote call. In essence, if yk_promote were to be statically inlined into a function which ykllvm determines doesn’t need to be traced, odd things happen, and so ykllvm throws a static error. In this case, the function that “should” contain the yk_promote can get inlined in multiple paths, one of which falls foul of this check. A hacky fix is to pull the promote out into a function which isn’t statically inlined27. I then did a second PR to inline range construction and iteration.

You may notice that in both of these PRs I have marked a much larger number of functions yk_indirect_inline than I have benchmark evidence for. The reason for this is a variant of something I mentioned above: my experience of indirect call sites is that either nearly all targets benefit from indirect inlining or none do. This clearly isn’t an iron law of the universe, but what it means is that I tend to look at all the possible targets, and mark them as yk_indirect_inline if they look sensible. So far, I have rarely regretted doing so.

Collectively these two PRs drive json’s performance down to 10.41s, though the effect on deltablue was too small to say anything either way. As I get further into optimising an interpreter for yk this is common: not all benchmarks benefit from all optimisations.

Wrapping up

At this point, you’ve probably got a good sense of how I approach ykifying an interpreter. I raised a few more PRs before realising that I wasn’t going to add much useful conceptually to this post: it was time to finish this stage of work off and write it up.

Before I started this little journey, I wasn’t entirely sure if yk would work at all – let alone “well”! – on an interpreter the size and complexity of CPython. The early stages didn’t entirely dispel my worries: there were lots of missing pieces, and quite a few bugs, that needed fixing in yk for ykcpython to work at all. The fact that ykcpython does work, and works fairly well, is proof that at least one big, complex, interpreter can be ykified with relative ease — and that it can be surprisingly competitive on performance.

Of course, I am lucky in many ways. yk already had decent foundations, thanks to several people’s hard work. The tier 2 interpreter in CPython made my life a lot easier than it might otherwise have been. Small benchmarks, like the ones I’ve used in this post, tend to flatter (meta-)tracing as a JIT compiling technique. And when it comes to ykifying interpreters, well, I’ve been round the block a few times.

But I don’t want to completely underplay things. 3-4 days isn’t that long to spend on an interpreter like CPython. It will take a lot longer than that – even with the wonder of LLMs to speed up the journey – to do a thorough job and squeeze all the juice that ykcpython can expose to yk. Similarly, I have only looked at a handful of benchmarks: it’s unlikely that ykcpython will magically speed up a wide range of programs yet, as there will be many other parts of CPython that need to be considered for optimisation. A lot of this will not be rocket science, but it is work, and not all of it can yet be automated.

I also haven’t made any performance optimisations (yet!) to yk for ykcpython specifically (though I have fixed a couple of bottlenecks that I had previously been able to ignore). In particular, one thing I am entirely confident in is that ykcpython will generate HIR patterns that yk doesn’t yet optimise effectively: fixing those will improve ykcpython’s performance for free, possibly quite a bit. Even without that, ykcpython has highlighted additional bottlenecks in yk that had never previously been an issue: each time one of those is fixed, ykcpython will magically get faster.

In a sense, this is one of the nice things that yk offers: improvements to yk nearly always benefit every ykified interpreter. It’s why I could bring ykcpython up to speed in a short period of time: I wasn’t writing a JIT compiler from scratch, I was reusing a generic toolkit. For example, the various missing pieces and bugs that ykcpython highlighted in yk will almost certainly make ykifying the next interpreter that bit easier — and hopefully future improvements to yk will benefit ykcpython even further!

Since then we’ve applied yk to more interpreters, fixed various bugs, and improved performance notably. Towards the end of October I showed some data where on our benchmark suite1 yklua is 2× faster than the PUC Lua interpreter it takes as a base. I was quite pleased with myself until someone brought me down to earth by asking “how do you know if this works for large interpreters?” It’s a fair question: PUC Lua is at least an order of magnitude smaller2 than CPython or CRuby and who’s to say if it would work with much bigger interpreters? A lot has changed since then, and a quick LLM experiment got far enough to suggest it would be worth looking again. Happily, having taken a deeper look, CPython not only works when adapted for yk as ykcpython3, but there are meaningful performance gains to be had — not only relative to normal CPython, but also relative to Python’s experimental JIT4. On each row the fastest entry(s) are shown in bold. A simple summary of the table is: ykcpython is faster than cpython on every benchmark except DeltaBlue (where it’s about 2.5% slower); and faster than cpython_jit on 8 out of 13 benchmarks. The point of this post is not to pretend that ykcpython is in any way ready for people to use — it definitely is not! Nor is it to pretend that one can expect performance on a wider set of programs to be as good as the numbers above — it definitely won’t! My view is that benchmark suite performance is a hoop to jump through rather than an end in itself: a system which benchmarks well might perform poorly in the real world; but a system which benchmarks poorly nearly always performs poorly in the real world. Rather, I wanted to use this post as a way of showing what it’s like to adapt an interpreter for yk5: the stages I went through; and to give a sense of how the just under 450LoC I added were enough to achieve a meaningful effect. Luckily I had a sense that this might be a useful journey, so I was able to write enough stuff down to be able to flesh out this full post. A quick refresher If you haven’t read the earlier yk post, here’s a very brief refresher. Given a lightly modified C interpreter6 as input, yk produces a VM with a meta-tracing JIT compiler as output7. yk doesn’t aim to produce the fastest possible JIT compiling language implementation: rather, it aims to make the language implementation you know and love somewhat faster while retaining 100% compatibility. Put another way a “ykified” interpreter is a fork of the existing C version of the interpreter, with (hopefully!) a handful of adjustments. As with any meta-tracing JIT compiler, yk identifies hot loops in the guest language (e.g. Lua or Python), and traces the interpreter (i.e. records what the C code is executing while it is interpreting the guest language). It then optimises those traces and converts them to machine code. yk requires interpreters to tell it where potential loops in the guest language are via the YkLocation struct. Optionally – though if you want to get good performance, definitely necessary! – interpreter authors can add optimisation hints that embed knowledge about the language or its common idioms of use such as “at this point this seemingly dynamic value almost never changes”. In general, working out where to put YkLocations is relatively easy, but working out where to put hints requires a much greater understanding of the interpreter, and careful measurement to understand which do and don’t help. The challenge I face when adapting an interpreter for yk is that I rarely know the interpreter well, if at all. Rather than trying to do everything at once, I have learnt to start off as simple as possible: I try and do the minimum changes that lead to some traces being recorded and compiled to machine code. This can be trickier than it seems: I’ve got to understand the build system8, and work out where to put some semi-sensible YkLocations. I’ve also learnt to make sure that the language’s test suite works from this very first step: keeping it working thereafter is not only much easier, but it lessens the number of times one attempts optimisations that are unsound. For a simple interpreter, you might get a basic JIT compiler from an interpreter with fewer than 10LoC (Lines-of-Code) changed. For somewhat bigger interpreters, a few more changes tend to be necessary. For example, yk doesn’t like “threaded” interpreters that use goto between opcodes, because it doesn’t give it enough opportunities to intercede and see what’s going on. Fortunately, such changes are not generally too big. Finding the right starting point Since it had been a long time since I looked at CPython’s internals9, I started with the part I was vaguely familiar with. As I later discovered, this is now called the “tier 1” interpreter. Quickly hacking in support for yk highlighted several missing things in yk (from basic atomic loads to not-implemented-bit-widths in sub, minor incompatibilities (e.g. reading an environment variable after a CPython test had wiped it), and flat out bugs (from stackmap fixes to not doing silly things after fork). Fixing all those took me around a week and a half; I’m not going to talk about them in detail in this post, because they’re generic fixes that aren’t ykcpython specific. My adaption of the tier 1 interpreter is deliberately minimalistic. Most of the changes in the 200LoC diff are small one-offs that aren’t hugely interesting: we need CPython to use its (builtin but non-default) switch-based interpreter; and yk uses a shadow stack, so CPython’s C stack resizing needs to take that into account too. The most interesting thing I did was to add YkLocations at backwards jump opcodes, which I expected to be enough for some half-sensible traces to be created. I wasn’t expecting this first version of ykcpython to be faster than CPython – if nothing else, it contained almost no optimisation hints – but it was much slower than I expected. It was definitely creating traces, and they were executing correctly – the test suite passed, albeit taking more memory than I’d like10 – but something clearly wasn’t right. Fortunately, it didn’t take very long to work out what. 4 years ago, CPython added support for quickening under the heading of “specialisation”. Quickening is a simple, clever technique for improving interpreter performance that rewrites “generic” opcodes (e.g. “add objects”) to “specialised”, faster, opcodes (e.g. “add two ints”) when possible, deoptimising back to the generic opcodes if necessary. I tend to think of quickening as giving a decent portion of the benefit of a JIT compiler without all the bother of generating machine code11. The problem for yk is that sometimes a program’s opcodes can transition between specialised and unspecialised opcodes a large number of times, and the simple way I’d added yk support meant that each transition implicitly threw away the associated trace and created a new one. In most cases, traces weren’t used long enough to overcome the cost of creating them. There are techniques which can overcome this problem, and I did briefly experiment with them, but I then recalled a conversation I had with some CPython developers last year. A quick look inside CPython confirmed my recollection: CPython contains a “tier 2” interpreter as well. This isn’t a completely new interpreter; rather it is an alternative implementation of core parts of the main interpreter loop, mostly intended for CPython’s experimental JIT compiler. A very quick experiment later suggested that the tier 2 interpreter was – at least at a basic level – a better fit for yk12. I thus ripped out the tier 1 support and added support for yk in the tier 2 interpreter. Happily, tier 2 support is even easier than tier 1 support, consisting of a mere 80 LoC. To give you a quick idea of what yk support looks like, here’s the part that attaches YkLocations13 to the (start of) loops: for (uint32_t i = 0; i < executor->code_size; i++) { const _PyUOpInstruction *uop = &executor->trace[i]; if (_PyUop_Uncached[uop->opcode] == _JUMP_TO_TOP) { uint16_t target = uop_get_jump_target(uop); if (yk_location_is_null(executor->yk_locs[target])) { executor->yk_locs[target] = yk_location_new(); } } } For the rest of this post, I’m going to be using yk and the tier 2 interpreter as the starting point for ykcpython. What’s being benchmarked When optimising any language implementation, it’s important to know where its performance sits in the wider performance landscape. To understand how ykcpython was doing, I used two other baselines: “stock” CPython; and CPython with the experimental JIT. I configured cpython as follows: CC=clang-21 CXX=clang++-21 \ ./configure \ --enable-optimizations \ --with-lto Note that I’m deliberately using the same version of LLVM for both cpython and cpython_jit because the latter requires LLVM-21. ykllvm – the fork of LLVM used in yk – is based off a version of LLVM about 6 months later than LLVM-21. That might slightly distort comparisons, but it’s a small enough difference that the effects hopefully are fairly minor. Bearing that in mind, ykcpython is configured as follows: ../configure \ --without-computed-gotos \ --without-tail-call-interp \ --enable-experimental-jit=interpreter \ --without-ensurepip I used our fork14 of the AWFY benchmark suite, simply because I know how to run it without thinking. The next challenge is to define a metric, or metrics, to report performance. Every metric has the potential to mislead and many are difficult to understand. In my opinion, the least worst single metric is wall-clock time: how long does my program take to run from start to finish? This doesn’t capture everything we want to know, but it captures a lot, and it’s easy to understand. Most importantly this metric implicitly includes start-up and warm-up time. In other words I’m deliberately choosing a timing metric which tends to favour normal interpreters and “penalise” JIT compilers. To somewhat offset that, we run each AWFY benchmark for 10 in-process iterations (i.e. run the whole benchmark in a for 0..10 loop) so that we also get some sense of how optimisation benefits longer-running programs. The big performance table at the start of this post uses a custom benchmark runner on an idle machine. All the timings from now on in the post are from me running time once as a normal user without being too careful if the machine is completely idle or not: when starting to optimise an interpreter, it’s not practical to wait an hour to benchmark every change on many benchmarks, when the effects are generally quite large15. My first port of call when optimising an interpreter is to tackle interpreter dispatch. When an interpreter is executing a program, it continually asks “what is the opcode of the current instruction? Is it an add or a sub or …?” and then it dispatches to the code that performs the appropriate action. It’s probable that a large chunk of that 20KLoC of HIR is the interpreter loading an opcode from memory and checking what kind it is. yk’s trace optimiser has various classic compiler tricks up its sleeve, but in this case they don’t really help, because in most cases between the same instruction being loaded twice from memory, some other code will be called that yk has to assume might have mutated that memory. This isn’t unnecessary conservatism: Python programs really can mutate their function’s instructions! I was particularly lucky because the tier2 interpreter uses “executors” which are traces of (optimised) instructions. Those instructions are immutable in the context of a given executor: should a Python function’s instructions change, any associated executors will be invalidated. That means that we can attach a simple monotonically increasing integer code ID to a _PyExecutorObject and know that for a given code ID, an opcode at index I will always be the same. This allows us to use the single most effective optimisation hint in yk: idempotent functions. In essence, an idempotent function says “for the same inputs this function will always produce the same output”18. “Always” here really means “always”! Idempotent is a very strong guarantee that yk cannot help you uphold: if you fail to do so, your system will go wrong in weird ways. Although yk provides a helper yk_idempotent_load function, we need something more specialised. Fortunately it’s not hard to write what we need: __attribute__((yk_idempotent)) uint16_t idempotent_load_opcode(uint64_t code_id, const _PyUOpInstruction *pc) { __asm__ volatile("" : "+r"(code_id)); return pc->opcode; } Unsurprisingly, the yk_idempotent attribute tells yk that idempotent_load_opcode is an idempotent function. That means that if, in a particular trace, the function is called with parameters that are constant values then yk can remove the idempotent function call and replace it with its output. The __asm__ line is there to encourage LLVM not to inline the function19 (if the function is inlined, yk no longer knows there is anything idempotent there). Using this requires changing just a few lines in the core interpreter loop. The most important lines are simply this: yk_promote(next_uop); yk_promote_code_id(yk_code_id); uopcode = idempotent_load_opcode(yk_code_id, next_uop); Promotion (e.g. yk_promote)20 says “this variable is expected to be semi-constant: record its concrete value and specialise the trace to it, but insert a guard in case that value later changes”. Imagine I have yk_promote(x) and when a trace is later recorded, x happens to be 3. The trace will record guard true (x == 3): if on later runs x is not 3, the guard will fail and the trace will deoptimise; if the guard succeeds we know henceforth that x is definitely 3. In other words, in the context of the traces we’re recording, yk will see calls to idempotent_load_opcode with constant arguments, allowing it to replace the function call with a constant result. The point of this isn’t just to remove the cost of a load: rather, exposing constant data to yk’s trace optimiser allows it to do a much better job of optimising traces. Code needs to be traced to be optimised However, before we get carried away, this isn’t enough to make all benchmarks magically quicker. I have learnt from experience to rotate between benchmarks to avoid over-training22. In this case I decided to look at the deltablue benchmark, which I know from yklua can be a tough target. The situation in ykcpython turned out to be worse than I expected: cpython takes 7.67s, cpython_jit takes 6.20s, and ykcpython (with our idempotent change) takes 37.51s. Ouch! My next port of call is to run YKD_LOG=2 which prints warnings if a trace can’t be compiled. Sure enough: $ ykcpython harness.py DeltaBlue 10 12000 Starting DeltaBlue benchmark ... yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long yk-warning: stop-tracing-aborted: Trace too long DeltaBlue: iterations=1 runtime: 3362822us yk-warning: trace-compilation-aborted: Unimplemented: '%188 = atomicrmw or ptr %187, i64 16 seq_cst, align 8' ... For now I’m going to skip “trace too long”. In essence yk has a fixed limit for “this trace looks to be so long that it’s probably not useful”. The limit was too low, so I increased it unilaterally before doing the work for this post. Exactly what the right value is I don’t know. Indeed, I think that this crude heuristic probably needs replacing with something more sophisticated: doing that is a problem for another day. Let’s move onto the “unimplemented” warning: I haven’t got around to implementing complex atomic instructions yet, so as soon as one of those is encountered, yk has no choice but to give up on that trace entirely. If it happens to be a hot part of a benchmark, that can absolutely kill performance. In this case, happily, the atomicrmw warnings just so happened to come from functions which we really don’t want to inline into the trace anyway. One of tracing’s virtues is that it aggressively inlines functions, but that can inline checks which fail too often on subsequent executions. For example, one function we inline by default is _PyObject_GC_Link which checks to see if enough objects have been allocated for garbage collection to be worth scheduling. If we’re unlucky, we may trace an iteration of a loop which happens to schedule garbage collection: in nearly every subsequent execution, the resulting guard will fail, and we’ll take a somewhat slower path. The solution here is to mark such functions as yk_outline: __attribute__((yk_outline)) void _PyObject_GC_Link(PyObject *op) { ... } Functions marked yk_outline become calls in a trace. There are probably a number of functions which should be marked as yk_outline, but I marked the two that happened to cause the aborted warnings and that also obviously we don’t want to include in a trace anyway. Doing so improved execution time to 36.63s (about 2.5% faster), so they’re clearly not the major cause of the slowdown in this case. Just when I was starting to fret, profiling execution showed that, to my surprise, deltablue was only spending about half its running time in JIT-compiled code, where one would expect it to be spending 90%+. It turns out that the main reason for this is that not all executors have a _JUMP_TO_TOP opcode and weren’t being traced. My quick fix was to add a YkLocation at the first opcode in an executor. The one line fix does just that: it means that yk starts tracing as soon as it enters an executor. Doing so improves deltablue’s execution time to 8.64s (4.23× faster than before). That’s still 1.13× CPython, but it’s a lot better than before! At the time I made this change I didn’t fully think about how adding a YkLocation at the start of an executor might interact with the YkLocation already added to _JUMP_TO_TOP. As luck would have it, I accidentally stumbled on a reasonable combination: _JUMP_TO_TOP tends to jump to the instruction at index 1. Still, I suspect that there might be a better way to add YkLocations to executors, but one can’t solve every problem all at once: it’s time to move onto the next thing! Further into interpreter dispatch Our earlier use of idempotent loads made such a huge impact on interpreter dispatch that it’s easy to overlook that it was a simple, shallow, change: it only optimised loading an instruction’s opcode kind. Instructions contain a number of other fields that are equally amenable to idempotent loading. There are various ways one can go about optimising these additional fields. I could, for example, have replaced the definitions of some static functions in header files. To keep things simple, I defined a macro which can generate the two-parameter functions we need, and then nobbled some other macros to call it at appropriate points. With the resulting change deltablue’s performance improves to 8.09s — we’re now within 10% of cpython’s performance. Unrolling As we saw earlier, not all functions are good candidates for inlining into a trace. yk has a very simple heuristic – stolen shamelessly from RPython/PyPy – which is to mark functions containing loops as “outlined”. In other words, if C calls a function f() and f contains for (...) { ... } then yk will not inline calls to f. The fundamental reason not to inline functions-with-loops is that tracing unrolls loops, and that tends not to be a good idea. First, some loops execute vast numbers of iterations, which would cause counter-productively-long traces. Second, loops’ iterations are often controlled by dynamic, ever-changing values: unrolling would specialise the trace to just one of those values, giving suboptimal performance on every other value. There are however a small number of functions in an interpreter which we actively want to unroll. Typically those functions’ loops satisfy two properties: they only run a small number of iterations; and the number of iterations depends on an aspect of the user’s program that changes rarely. For example, a function called unpack_args(int num_args) which contains for (int i=0; i<num_args; i++) would be an excellent candidate, since it probably unpacks the same number of parameters every time it is called at the same place in a trace. yk thus provides a yk_unroll attribute, which informs yk that a function that might otherwise be outlined should in fact be inlined and its loops unrolled. Rather than slog through every function in CPython looking for candidates, I did a simple grep/sort in hir to see which (implicitly non-inlined) C functions appear most often in traces23: $ YKD_LOG_IR=/tmp/l1:hir ykcpython harness.py Json 10 100 ... $ rg call /tmp/l1|grep "@"|cut -d "@" -f 2|sort|uniq -c|sort -n 2 PyLong_FromLong 6 _Py_HandlePending 6 do_lookup 24 _PyList_FromStackRefStealOnSuccess 50 _PyEvalFramePushAndInit 50 _PyObject_GC_Link 50 _PyObject_InitInlineValues 263 PyLong_FromSsize_t 1035 _PyFrame_Initialize.5328 1158 _PyFrame_ClearLocals 1194 bcmp bcmp is the standard libc function: all of the other functions are in CPython itself. Not all of those functions will have loops in them, but the chances are that most do. What I do in such a situation is go down (or, depending how you look at it, up) the list and look at the code in each function. I did that for a couple of benchmarks to ensure I got some coverage of common functions. The two most commonly called CPython functions immediately looked like good candidates. _PyFrame_Initialize is the most obvious of the two, containing almost exactly the pattern I most like to match on: _PyFrame_Initialize(..., int null_locals_from, ...) { ... for (int i = null_locals_from; i < code->co_nlocalsplus; i++) { frame->localsplus[i] = PyStackRef_NULL; } ... } _PyFrame_ClearLocals is slightly trickier: it contains a while loop involving pointer arithmetic, but it didn’t take me long to convince myself that it was a good candidate. Earlier we made _PyObject_GC_Link not inlineable, so we don’t want to reverse that! Similarly, do_lookup looks values up in a dictionary, so we want to keep that outlined: it depends on an often-changing dynamic value. PyLong_FromSsize_t and PyLong_FromLong were harder to judge. These functions’ inner loops depend on dynamic values, but my best guess is that they tend to be fairly stable in practice. I will be keeping an eye on these functions in the future, because I only have medium confidence that I made the right initial call. As these examples suggest, I am generally fairly cautious about adding yk_unroll: inappropriate placings can easily help one benchmark and make many others worse. I thus tend to only mark one or two functions as yk_unroll, benchmark, and then move on. In this case, I did 5 small PRs, with the end effect that json went from 11.52s to 10.85s. Indirect inlining In general most function calls in C are direct: f() calls a function called f. However a minority of functions are indirect: f is a generic pointer whose value can be any compatible function. This is commonly used in interpreters to allow run-time dispatch to type specific code. By default, yk cannot inline through indirect function calls, because without knowing exactly what pointer is being called, it can’t reliably reconstruct the path that execution took24. Fortunately, we already have the tool we need to solve this problem: yk_promote! If yk sees an indirect function call with a constant pointer it knows exactly what function is being called and can inline as normal. The common pattern I use is: function_type f = ...; if (!yk_is_interpreting()) yk_promote(f); (f)(...); yk_is_interpreting() is true during “normal” interpretation; false during tracing; and (because it’s a constant false) removed during tracing. In other words, yk_promote is only called during the tracing phase. yk_is_interpreting() is fairly fast (much faster than yk_promote()) so this idiom is a small but useful performance win. However, there is often a second problem. yk only puts the tracing machinery into a function if it can statically prove that it is reachable from a traceable path. Commonly, functions called from indirect calls cannot be statically proven to be traceable and thus they still leave an outlined call in the trace. We can solve that with the yk_indirect_inline function which tells yk “this function can be reached from an indirect call and should be considered for tracing”25. Profiling a couple of benchmarks quickly showed several potential candidates26. My experience is that not all indirect call sites are good targets for promotion: for example, of the interpreters I’ve looked at so far, inlining malloc and free indirect calls has rarely been profitable. However, I quickly alighted upon a couple of promising candidates. Let’s start with the less promising, but easier to explain, one: benchmarks like deltablue and json call len on lists and strings. Simplifying slightly, sq_length is a pointer to a function inside a CPython type, so this becomes an indirect call in traces. In the case of len([...]) the function that’s ultimately called is list_length: static Py_ssize_t list_length(PyObject *a) { return PyList_GET_SIZE(a); } where PyList_GET_SIZE boils down (slightly elided) to a simple load a->ob_size. That’s the sort of code that yk loves to see inlined in a trace! The resulting PR has to do a slightly annoying dance to make yk accept the yk_promote call. In essence, if yk_promote were to be statically inlined into a function which ykllvm determines doesn’t need to be traced, odd things happen, and so ykllvm throws a static error. In this case, the function that “should” contain the yk_promote can get inlined in multiple paths, one of which falls foul of this check. A hacky fix is to pull the promote out into a function which isn’t statically inlined27. I then did a second PR to inline range construction and iteration. You may notice that in both of these PRs I have marked a much larger number of functions yk_indirect_inline than I have benchmark evidence for. The reason for this is a variant of something I mentioned above: my experience of indirect call sites is that either nearly all targets benefit from indirect inlining or none do. This clearly isn’t an iron law of the universe, but what it means is that I tend to look at all the possible targets, and mark them as yk_indirect_inline if they look sensible. So far, I have rarely regretted doing so. Collectively these two PRs drive json’s performance down to 10.41s, though the effect on deltablue was too small to say anything either way. As I get further into optimising an interpreter for yk this is common: not all benchmarks benefit from all optimisations. Wrapping up At this point, you’ve probably got a good sense of how I approach ykifying an interpreter. I raised a few more PRs before realising that I wasn’t going to add much useful conceptually to this post: it was time to finish this stage of work off and write it up. Before I started this little journey, I wasn’t entirely sure if yk would work at all – let alone “well”! – on an interpreter the size and complexity of CPython. The early stages didn’t entirely dispel my worries: there were lots of missing pieces, and quite a few bugs, that needed fixing in yk for ykcpython to work at all. The fact that ykcpython does work, and works fairly well, is proof that at least one big, complex, interpreter can be ykified with relative ease — and that it can be surprisingly competitive on performance. Of course, I am lucky in many ways. yk already had decent foundations, thanks to several people’s hard work. The tier 2 interpreter in CPython made my life a lot easier than it might otherwise have been. Small benchmarks, like the ones I’ve used in this post, tend to flatter (meta-)tracing as a JIT compiling technique. And when it comes to ykifying interpreters, well, I’ve been round the block a few times. But I don’t want to completely underplay things. 3-4 days isn’t that long to spend on an interpreter like CPython. It will take a lot longer than that – even with the wonder of LLMs to speed up the journey – to do a thorough job and squeeze all the juice that ykcpython can expose to yk. Similarly, I have only looked at a handful of benchmarks: it’s unlikely that ykcpython will magically speed up a wide range of programs yet, as there will be many other parts of CPython that need to be considered for optimisation. A lot of this will not be rocket science, but it is work, and not all of it can yet be automated. I also haven’t made any performance optimisations (yet!) to yk for ykcpython specifically (though I have fixed a couple of bottlenecks that I had previously been able to ignore). In particular, one thing I am entirely confident in is that ykcpython will generate HIR patterns that yk doesn’t yet optimise effectively: fixing those will improve ykcpython’s performance for free, possibly quite a bit. Even without that, ykcpython has highlighted additional bottlenecks in yk that had never previously been an issue: each time one of those is fixed, ykcpython will magically get faster. In a sense, this is one of the nice things that yk offers: improvements to yk nearly always benefit every ykified interpreter. It’s why I could bring ykcpython up to speed in a short period of time: I wasn’t writing a JIT compiler from scratch, I was reusing a generic toolkit. For example, the various missing pieces and bugs that ykcpython highlighted in yk will almost certainly make ykifying the next interpreter that bit easier — and hopefully future improvements to yk will benefit ykcpython even further! blocks.html_en: If you haven’t read the earlier yk post, here’s a very brief refresher. Given a lightly modified C interpreter6 as input, yk produces a VM with a meta-tracing JIT compiler as output7. yk doesn’t aim to produce the fastest possible JIT compiling language implementation: rather, it aims to make the language implementation you know and love somewhat faster while retaining 100% compatibility. Put another way a “ykified” interpreter is a fork of the existing C version of the interpreter, with (hopefully!) a handful of adjustments.

blocks.html_en: As with any meta-tracing JIT compiler, yk identifies hot loops in the guest language (e.g. Lua or Python), and traces the interpreter (i.e. records what the C code is executing while it is interpreting the guest language). It then optimises those traces and converts them to machine code.

blocks.html_en: yk requires interpreters to tell it where potential loops in the guest language are via the YkLocation struct. Optionally – though if you want to get good performance, definitely necessary! – interpreter authors can add optimisation hints that embed knowledge about the language or its common idioms of use such as “at this point this seemingly dynamic value almost never changes”. In general, working out where to put YkLocations is relatively easy, but working out where to put hints requires a much greater understanding of the interpreter, and careful measurement to understand which do and don’t help.

blocks.html_en: The challenge I face when adapting an interpreter for yk is that I rarely know the interpreter well, if at all. Rather than trying to do everything at once, I have learnt to start off as simple as possible: I try and do the minimum changes that lead to some traces being recorded and compiled to machine code. This can be trickier than it seems: I’ve got to understand the build system8, and work out where to put some semi-sensible YkLocations. I’ve also learnt to make sure that the language’s test suite works from this very first step: keeping it working thereafter is not only much easier, but it lessens the number of times one attempts optimisations that are unsound.

blocks.html_en: Fortunately, it didn’t take very long to work out what. 4 years ago, CPython added support for quickening under the heading of “specialisation”. Quickening is a simple, clever technique for improving interpreter performance that rewrites “generic” opcodes (e.g. “add objects”) to “specialised”, faster, opcodes (e.g. “add two ints”) when possible, deoptimising back to the generic opcodes if necessary. I tend to think of quickening as giving a decent portion of the benefit of a JIT compiler without all the bother of generating machine code11. The problem for yk is that sometimes a program’s opcodes can transition between specialised and unspecialised opcodes a large number of times, and the simple way I’d added yk support meant that each transition implicitly threw away the associated trace and created a new one. In most cases, traces weren’t used long enough to overcome the cost of creating them.

blocks.html_en: My first port of call when optimising an interpreter is to tackle interpreter dispatch. When an interpreter is executing a program, it continually asks “what is the opcode of the current instruction? Is it an add or a sub or …?” and then it dispatches to the code that performs the appropriate action. It’s probable that a large chunk of that 20KLoC of HIR is the interpreter loading an opcode from memory and checking what kind it is. yk’s trace optimiser has various classic compiler tricks up its sleeve, but in this case they don’t really help, because in most cases between the same instruction being loaded twice from memory, some other code will be called that yk has to assume might have mutated that memory. This isn’t unnecessary conservatism: Python programs really can mutate their function’s instructions!

content_html_zh:
Earlier this year I wrote a post on yk, which can automatically add JIT compilers to C interpreters. Since then we’ve applied yk to more interpreters, fixed various bugs, and improved performance notably. Towards the end of October I showed some data where on our benchmark suite1 yklua is 2× faster than the PUC Lua interpreter it takes as a base.

I was quite pleased with myself until someone brought me down to earth by asking “how do you know if this works for large interpreters?” It’s a fair question: PUC Lua is at least an order of magnitude smaller2 than CPython or CRuby and who’s to say if it would work with much bigger interpreters? We had looked at CPython a year or so ago, but at that point yk was missing several obvious things that CPython would need, so we quickly moved on. A lot has changed since then, and a quick LLM experiment got far enough to suggest it would be worth looking again.

Happily, having taken a deeper look, CPython not only works when adapted for yk as ykcpython3, but there are meaningful performance gains to be had — not only relative to normal CPython, but also relative to Python’s experimental JIT4. Roughly speaking, this is the result of 3-4 days’ work on ykcpython directly; there was a separate week and a half of generic yk bug fixing necessary to get to the point that I could look at ykcpython itself.

Here are the “final” numbers from my brief odyssey on ykcpython and the AWFY benchmark suite:

Times are in seconds (lower is better) with means and 99% confidence intervals bootstrapped from 30 process executions, running on a 64 core AMD EPYC 7773X Debian machine in performance mode (download the repeatable experiment and the raw data). On each row the fastest entry(s) are shown in bold.

A simple summary of the table is: ykcpython is faster than cpython on every benchmark except DeltaBlue (where it’s about 2.5% slower); and faster than cpython_jit on 8 out of 13 benchmarks.

The point of this post is not to pretend that ykcpython is in any way ready for people to use — it definitely is not! Nor is it to pretend that one can expect performance on a wider set of programs to be as good as the numbers above — it definitely won’t! My view is that benchmark suite performance is a hoop to jump through rather than an end in itself: a system which benchmarks well might perform poorly in the real world; but a system which benchmarks poorly nearly always performs poorly in the real world.

Rather, I wanted to use this post as a way of showing what it’s like to adapt an interpreter for yk5: the stages I went through; and to give a sense of how the just under 450LoC I added were enough to achieve a meaningful effect. Luckily I had a sense that this might be a useful journey, so I was able to write enough stuff down to be able to flesh out this full post.

A quick refresher

If you haven’t read the earlier yk post, here’s a very brief refresher. Given a lightly modified C interpreter6 as input, yk produces a VM with a meta-tracing JIT compiler as output7. yk doesn’t aim to produce the fastest possible JIT compiling language implementation: rather, it aims to make the language implementation you know and love somewhat faster while retaining 100% compatibility. Put another way a “ykified” interpreter is a fork of the existing C version of the interpreter, with (hopefully!) a handful of adjustments.

As with any meta-tracing JIT compiler, yk identifies hot loops in the guest language (e.g. Lua or Python), and traces the interpreter (i.e. records what the C code is executing while it is interpreting the guest language). It then optimises those traces and converts them to machine code.

yk requires interpreters to tell it where potential loops in the guest language are via the YkLocation struct. Optionally – though if you want to get good performance, definitely necessary! – interpreter authors can add optimisation hints that embed knowledge about the language or its common idioms of use such as “at this point this seemingly dynamic value almost never changes”. In general, working out where to put YkLocations is relatively easy, but working out where to put hints requires a much greater understanding of the interpreter, and careful measurement to understand which do and don’t help.

The challenge I face when adapting an interpreter for yk is that I rarely know the interpreter well, if at all. Rather than trying to do everything at once, I have learnt to start off as simple as possible: I try and do the minimum changes that lead to some traces being recorded and compiled to machine code. This can be trickier than it seems: I’ve got to understand the build system8, and work out where to put some semi-sensible YkLocations. I’ve also learnt to make sure that the language’s test suite works from this very first step: keeping it working thereafter is not only much easier, but it lessens the number of times one attempts optimisations that are unsound.

For a simple interpreter, you might get a basic JIT compiler from an interpreter with fewer than 10LoC (Lines-of-Code) changed. For somewhat bigger interpreters, a few more changes tend to be necessary. For example, yk doesn’t like “threaded” interpreters that use goto between opcodes, because it doesn’t give it enough opportunities to intercede and see what’s going on. Fortunately, such changes are not generally too big.

Finding the right starting point

Since it had been a long time since I looked at CPython’s internals9, I started with the part I was vaguely familiar with. As I later discovered, this is now called the “tier 1” interpreter. Quickly hacking in support for yk highlighted several missing things in yk (from basic atomic loads to not-implemented-bit-widths in sub, minor incompatibilities (e.g. reading an environment variable after a CPython test had wiped it), and flat out bugs (from stackmap fixes to not doing silly things after fork). Fixing all those took me around a week and a half; I’m not going to talk about them in detail in this post, because they’re generic fixes that aren’t ykcpython specific.

My adaption of the tier 1 interpreter is deliberately minimalistic. Most of the changes in the 200LoC diff are small one-offs that aren’t hugely interesting: we need CPython to use its (builtin but non-default) switch-based interpreter; and yk uses a shadow stack, so CPython’s C stack resizing needs to take that into account too. The most interesting thing I did was to add YkLocations at backwards jump opcodes, which I expected to be enough for some half-sensible traces to be created.

I wasn’t expecting this first version of ykcpython to be faster than CPython – if nothing else, it contained almost no optimisation hints – but it was much slower than I expected. It was definitely creating traces, and they were executing correctly – the test suite passed, albeit taking more memory than I’d like10 – but something clearly wasn’t right.

Fortunately, it didn’t take very long to work out what. 4 years ago, CPython added support for quickening under the heading of “specialisation”. Quickening is a simple, clever technique for improving interpreter performance that rewrites “generic” opcodes (e.g. “add objects”) to “specialised”, faster, opcodes (e.g. “add two ints”) when possible, deoptimising back to the generic opcodes if necessary. I tend to think of quickening as giving a decent portion of the benefit of a JIT compiler without all the bother of generating machine code11. The problem for yk is that sometimes a program’s opcodes can transition between specialised and unspecialised opcodes a large number of times, and the simple way I’d added yk support meant that each transition implicitly threw away the associated trace and created a new one. In most cases, traces weren’t used long enough to overcome the cost of creating them.

There are techniques which can overcome this problem, and I did briefly experiment with them, but I then recalled a conversation I had with some CPython developers last year. A quick look inside CPython confirmed my recollection: CPython contains a “tier 2” interpreter as well. This isn’t a completely new interpreter; rather it is an alternative implementation of core parts of the main interpreter loop, mostly intended for CPython’s experimental JIT compiler.

A very quick experiment later suggested that the tier 2 interpreter was – at least at a basic level – a better fit for yk12. I thus ripped out the tier 1 support and added support for yk in the tier 2 interpreter. Happily, tier 2 support is even easier than tier 1 support, consisting of a mere 80 LoC. To give you a quick idea of what yk support looks like, here’s the part that attaches YkLocations13 to the (start of) loops:

for (uint32_t i = 0; i < executor->code_size; i++) {
  const _PyUOpInstruction *uop = &executor->trace[i];
  if (_PyUop_Uncached[uop->opcode] == _JUMP_TO_TOP) {
    uint16_t target = uop_get_jump_target(uop);
    if (yk_location_is_null(executor->yk_locs[target])) {
      executor->yk_locs[target] = yk_location_new();
    }
  }
}

For the rest of this post, I’m going to be using yk and the tier 2 interpreter as the starting point for ykcpython.

What’s being benchmarked

When optimising any language implementation, it’s important to know where its performance sits in the wider performance landscape. To understand how ykcpython was doing, I used two other baselines: “stock” CPython; and CPython with the experimental JIT. I configured cpython as follows:

CC=clang-21 CXX=clang++-21 \
  ./configure \
  --enable-optimizations \
  --with-lto

Note that I’m deliberately using the same version of LLVM for both cpython and cpython_jit because the latter requires LLVM-21. ykllvm – the fork of LLVM used in yk – is based off a version of LLVM about 6 months later than LLVM-21. That might slightly distort comparisons, but it’s a small enough difference that the effects hopefully are fairly minor. Bearing that in mind, ykcpython is configured as follows:

../configure \
  --without-computed-gotos \
  --without-tail-call-interp \
  --enable-experimental-jit=interpreter \
  --without-ensurepip

I used our fork14 of the AWFY benchmark suite, simply because I know how to run it without thinking.

The next challenge is to define a metric, or metrics, to report performance. Every metric has the potential to mislead and many are difficult to understand. In my opinion, the least worst single metric is wall-clock time: how long does my program take to run from start to finish? This doesn’t capture everything we want to know, but it captures a lot, and it’s easy to understand.

Most importantly this metric implicitly includes start-up and warm-up time. In other words I’m deliberately choosing a timing metric which tends to favour normal interpreters and “penalise” JIT compilers. To somewhat offset that, we run each AWFY benchmark for 10 in-process iterations (i.e. run the whole benchmark in a for 0..10 loop) so that we also get some sense of how optimisation benefits longer-running programs.

The big performance table at the start of this post uses a custom benchmark runner on an idle machine. All the timings from now on in the post are from me running time once as a normal user without being too careful if the machine is completely idle or not: when starting to optimise an interpreter, it’s not practical to wait an hour to benchmark every change on many benchmarks, when the effects are generally quite large15.
